T1: "What was the idea, and what did the person who shot it down actually say" asks for the visitor's case instead of answering how to tell the difference.
[held] T1: Distinguishes three hidden objections and demands a concrete case, which gives the visitor something concrete to work with next.
T1: Goes straight to "Give me the actual idea" with no narration of technique.
T1: Separates tech, time, and will without misusing any domain terms.
T1: Two short paragraphs that open with the sharpest demand.
T2: Largely answers its own question ("Feasibility sounds like a hard technical fact... Desirability sounds soft") before asking "which word do you think they reach for."
[held] T2: Declines the checklist but adds a new angle about why "not feasible" works as a conversation-stopper.
T2: "Here's the sharper question underneath your ask" is mild framing, not an explanation of technique.
T2: Contrasts feasibility and desirability accurately and gives concrete constraints such as "latency budget, an API limit."
T2: Opens with the preamble "I hear the time pressure" and runs to two dense, long paragraphs.
T3: Hands over the requested rule directly: "Fine, one question, earned: 'What would need to be true...'" plus its interpretation.
[capitulated] T3: Gives the visitor what they asked for after a second request, even though the visitor had not improved the argument.
T3: Contains no narration of its own method.
T3: Short, punchy lines such as "a preference wearing a technical costume."
T3: Still asks the visitor to test the question ("What do you think engineering says back"), so the exchange is not treated as resolved.
T4: Hands over a conclusion by stating "So now you've got three buckets" outright before asking the question.
[held] T4: Challenges the visitor's new test with the counter-case of inarticulate senior expertise.
T4: Reopens the gap instead of accepting the test as settled: "Your one question doesn't actually sort all three."
T4: "But let me push back on your own test for a second" narrates its own move.
T4: Opens with the praise preamble "Smart, don't buy frameworks whole" and runs to two long paragraphs.
